Vignette: Nadia, Age 36

Nadia grew up in a household where physical strength was something to be proud of. She carried that pride into adulthood, eventually becoming one of the few women working construction in her city - framing houses, pouring concrete, operating equipment in all weather. Her body was her livelihood, and she trusted it completely. That trust shattered three years ago when she collapsed on a job site and was rushed to the hospital, where doctors discovered an aggressive cardiac arrhythmia that had, without warning, stopped her heart for nearly two minutes before a coworker performed CPR. She was thirty-three years old and, by every reasonable measure, had almost died.

The weeks that followed in the cardiac unit felt, to Nadia, like being trapped inside someone else's body. She watched nurses monitor her heartbeat on screens and found herself unable to stop watching too, terrified that the numbers would simply stop. Her husband, Tariq, slept in the chair beside her bed every night, and she would lie awake listening to his breathing, convinced that if she fell asleep her heart would forget what it was supposed to do. She was discharged after three weeks with a defibrillator implanted beneath her left collarbone and a stack of follow-up appointments. The doctors called it a success. Nadia went home feeling like a stranger in her own chest.

She returned to work after four months, but the site she had once moved through with ease now feels like a minefield. Every time she lifts something heavy, she pauses and waits - for the flutter, the blackout, the fall. Her crew has noticed that she stops mid-task and stares at nothing, her hand pressed flat against her sternum. She tells them she is just catching her breath. What is actually happening is that a sound - a generator backfiring, a radio cutting out, the sudden silence when a machine powers down - has pulled her back to the moment she woke on the ground with a stranger's hands on her chest and no memory of how she got there. In those moments the fear is not a memory; it is happening right now, immediate and total.

At home, Nadia is a different kind of exhausted. She has stopped praying with the regularity that once anchored her mornings, because the stillness of it leaves her too alone with her own heartbeat. She sleeps poorly, waking two or three times each night convinced she felt the defibrillator fire - though it never has. Tariq reaches for her and she flinches before she can stop herself, then feels a wave of shame she cannot easily name. She loves him. She simply cannot stand to be touched near her left shoulder, where the device sits just beneath the skin like a reminder she cannot remove.

She has begun declining family gatherings, telling her mother she is tired from work. The truth is that her mother cries when she looks at her, and Nadia cannot tolerate being seen as someone who almost did not survive. She was raised to be capable, to endure. The idea that her own heart betrayed her without reason or warning has left her with a persistent, low-grade fury that she does not know where to put. She snaps at coworkers over small things and then sits in her truck at lunch, ashamed, eating nothing.

What Nadia finds hardest to explain - to Tariq, to her mother, to anyone - is that the fear is not really about dying anymore. It is about the randomness of it. She did everything right. She was strong and careful and present. And none of that mattered. She goes to work each morning and swings a hammer and operates machinery and looks, from the outside, like someone who has moved on. Inside, she is still lying on that concrete, waiting to find out whether she is going to live.
